title: Witcher 3 designer says it wasn't easy to convince players its NPC simulation wasn't 'just fakery': 'People nowadays are interested in those kinds of details, and it really came to haunt us'
summary: "Today, if you said 'give me a Witcher 3 village that has eight houses', I could give you that in two hours."
body: It might seem silly to ask in our post-Red Dead horse testicles world , but how much exacting detail is too much? How much is not enough? Gamedev can go on forever if you don't prioritize the things that players actually notice, but if you're making an immersive fantasy RPG, it's critical that the intended illusions—bustling towns, lively taverns, festering dungeons, and so on—not shatter. This tightrope walk is something CDPR has gotten better at over the years, but it loomed over The Witcher 3's development, as CD Projekt Red's Philipp Weber told Edge Magazine (via Gamesradar ). The reason why is simple: wherever possible, gamers love to try and peek behind the curtain. "If a village only has eight houses, people will want to see if the people truly exist in the world or if it's just fakery," Weber told Edge. "Lots of people nowadays are interested in those kinds of details, and it really came to haunt us." "Today, if you said 'give me a Witcher 3 village that has eight houses', I could give you that in two hours," he said. But there was a time that "when it came to actually reacting to the player, there wasn't that much detail." An example case named in the article is that when…

title: The bigwigs who want AI-generated NPCs and writing think you're too dumb to appreciate a good story—don't prove them right
summary: The delight's in the details.
body: As I sit here, watching Saber Interactive's CEO have a normal one about how generative AI dialogue can totally improve videogames, I can't help but grit my teeth in the same, enamel-grinding fashion I have ever since companies like Ubisoft started promising a future with AI-powered "neo-NPCs." If you'd believe the hype, these things are potentially good on paper, right? We live in a development environment where the ambitions of big-budget open world games are far outstripping their cost—wouldn't it simply be marvellous if you could populate a world with infinite dialogue chains and storylines? In practice, the result is… pretty middling. While yes, some of the isolated tech demos we've seen have been impressive, the actual implementation of those we've seen in videogames, such as the life sim Seed , or Inzoi, which tried to pilot "smart Zois" , fell flat. Even when they're a source of entertainment, that fun is mostly found in the process of making them believe they're pregnant —and listen, I love toys. Putting aside my general distaste for generative AI, I don't think that every single videogame that comes out has to be a work of art. Toys are fine, you can smash action figures …

title: This Solitaire game is so tiny it can load from a QR code, which is just what I need in the age of massive games and expensive storage
summary: TinySol is a mini marvel.
body: At a time when game file sizes are growing ever larger and disk space is astonishingly expensive , I increasingly appreciate the value of a small game. And they don't come much smaller than TinySol, a solitaire game so diminutive that it can be loaded from a QR code. TinySol is the creation of vintage computer enthusiasts Classic Bits , and was stumbled upon by YouTuber LGR Blerbs at the VCF Southwest convention in Texas. In what sounds like the beginning of a horror film, Blerbs was randomly handed TinySol at a booth on a 5.25-inch floppy disk. Despite appearances, TinySol is a new(ish) game, having been in development since 2021. In the dot matrix-style manual that accompanies the hard copy, developer Classic Bits explains "I originally wanted a tiny game to shoehorn into ROM images for GRiD computers and that would leverage the sharp 640x400 AT&T 6300 monochrome video." Weighing in at a paltry 3 kilobytes, TinySol lets players enjoy three-card Klondike Solitaire with simple black & white graphics. The program is so compact that it can fit within a QR code, which can be decoded with a snippet of code written on TinySol's packaging. In the comments to Blerbs' video, Classic Bits …

title: Stalker 2's imminent free update aims to make the sequel more atmospheric and less relentlessly hostile: 'The Zone isn't one constant gunfight'
summary: The patch releases next week alongside the sequel's first story expansion.
body: You could tell that Stalker 2 was a true sequel to 2007's survivalist FPS in that it was as broken as it was brilliant. GSC Game World succeeded in delivering the seamless open world it has spent two decades striving toward, but players' exploration of Chornobyl's exclusion zone was hindered by bugs, broken quests, and more performance issues than a drunk orchestra. The sequel has received numerous massive patches already, but the biggest and—hopefully—best is yet to come. With the imminent arrival of the shooter's first story expansion , GSC has detailed the enormous 2.0 patch that will accompany the DLC. Named 'Back to the Zone', the 2.0 update will bring both a visual and mechanical refresh to Stalker 2 upon its release next week, as detailed by GSC in an article on its website . The headline change is an overhaul to the Zone's lighting, which GSC says it has altered to provide more varied conditions: "The sun still shines brightly outside, but now it plays differently across the environment on the ground—shadows and reflections included," GSC writers. body: Palworld went into full release in July after more than two years of early access, and it's going pretty well: A massive surge in concurrent players on Steam is slowly settling back down to Earth, but more than a month after that 1.0 launch it's still putting up numbers that haven't been seen since the early days of that early access rollout. Work on the game continues and there's more to come, but Pocketpair's publishing and communications head John "Bucky" Buckley recently warned that players should maybe temper their expectations about what's next. Buckley apparently set the bar higher than intended yesterday when he celebrated Palworld's "incredible" 1.0 launch by retweeting an image of a "Palworld v1.1 brainstorming session," adding, "time to get back to the grind!" title: The Epic Games Launcher will be available on Linux 'soon' says dev, after it's had a bit of work
summary: Another year of Linux PC gaming, perhaps?
body: Linux gaming has been rumbling along in the background for some time. However, this seems to be the year it reaches a wider audience, as proper Linux support has become a much-requested feature for many platforms. Next up is the Epic Games Store/Launcher, it seems, as an Epic dev has responded to a user query about Linux support with an emoji saying "soon." The conversation was spotted (and indeed, screenshotted) by Mr_Madafaka on Reddit. "But not for the preview release," says Onepercentnachos on the Epic Games Store Discord community server. "As you can imagine, we need to do more than simply have a build of the launcher that can run natively on Linux." Even some of our own team have made the leap into Linux in 2026 , mostly due to sheer malaise towards Windows 11 and its tiresome ways. Linux is far from a fresh new face in the gaming space, but Microsoft's previously ubiquitous OS seems to be losing ground. Valve is in the process of adding more handheld support to the Linux-based SteamOS , too, and the Steam Deck is extremely popular. "Stella who?" asked Matt Karch, "I had to ask Claude because I have never spoken to her or seen her. We have already said we are using AI for certain parts of the game and will update the Steam page once we have finalized the feature set." Karch also added that "it was always our intention to reveal this until Stella violated her confidentiality clause and revealed this before we were ready." Sacco, who claimed she was replaced "with ChatGPT" in 2023 , called the statement "remarkably pathetic for the CEO of any company to be making." You can read both parties' full statements in the articles linked above—the most recent development is that Saber Interactive has been seemingly pressed into adding a Steam AI disclaimer to the game's store page , which is present at the time of writing, but was notably not present when the game was put on the store on July 30. "We’re especially excited about the momentum we’re seeing with cloud games and kids games." Unhinged, as I mentioned, was developed by Night School and released just six weeks ago, on June 30. title: Stop Killing Games has joined a lawsuit against Sony's move to digital-only sales: 'You won't have any choice at all'
summary: Sony-only.
body: Sony's decision to stop selling physical disks for its games makes a certain kind of sense from a mercilessly realist point of view—I'd be a hypocrite if I, a person with the majority of my games on one platform (Steam), shook my fist and wept for the end of physical media. But aside from the sentimental concerns—which, honestly, I don't hold as any less important, there's more to life than money—there is a capitalist argument against the move, too, for both the consumer and the people who make videogames. If Sony ends physical disk sales, Sony decides how much a game on the PlayStation costs, forever. Such is the argument of one Dutch consumer group that's currently suing Sony for their proposed changes, stating last month that "no discs means no second-hand market and no alternative to the PlayStation Store, so from 2028, Sony alone decides what a game costs and even how long you are allowed to use it." At the very least, despite Steam's monolithic popularity, Valve's not capable of forcing anybody to use it. You can still use GOG or Itch.io or… Epic, if you really wanted to. The death of physical media for PC means something very different than the death of media for consoles. …

title: Videogame lawyer says it's become 'just boilerplate' this year to include no-AI clauses in contracts: 'It's not worth the legal liability'
summary: Looks like the law is finally catching up.
body: There's a problem with new technologies, in that cutting-edge technology develops quickly—in the span of years. Meanwhile, us human beings with our wet flesh bodies and our complicated bureaucracies and legal systems are glacially slow. You can see this playing out with generative AI. For a few years now, we've heard a lot of overexcitement from the videogame industry that AI is going to let smaller companies make bigger games, that soon you'll be able to generate your own concept art, your own music, your own videogame dialogue —and, of course, the deeply tedious phrase "democratising art". In actuality, generative AI is more of a plagiarism machine, often spitting out carbon copies and, even when it's not doing that, still requires countless copyrighted works ( which sometimes have to literally be burned ) to actually function. That legal heat has spooked videogame companies, so says lawyer Haley MacLean in an interview with our friends over at GamesRadar+ . MacLean, both a corporate IP lawyer and a videogame specialist at Voyer Law, tells the site that no-AI clauses are on the rise, particularly in the last year: "It's turned around, especially in the past year.
